newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yield jumps at Russian T-bill auction.
newsitem.headline: Yield jumps at Russian T-bill auction.

text.p: The average yield rose sharply at an auction of six-month Treasury bills on Wednesday as the finance ministry desperately sought cash to pay striking workers and to repay a maturing issue, dealers said.
Concern about President Boris Yeltsin's health also discouraged foreign investors.
But at another auction of three-month bills the average yield only rose slightly.
Dealers said a major bank, which they believed was the state savings bank Sberbank, had bought many of the three-month bills, helping hold down yields.
At the auction of six-month paper the average yield rose to 82.62 percent from 61.25 percent a week ago.
"The finance ministry needed the money badly and to repay a maturing issue too," said Oleg Surkov, head of securities operations department at Bank MFK.
"The central bank does not have the money and while they managed to carry out the first auction with the help of one bank, there was no one to buy at the second auction."
A sign of the finance ministry's need for cash was heavy selling of T-bills in the secondary market earlier this week. The central bank sold one trillion roubles worth of paper on Monday and Tuesday.
The finance ministry had to accept high yields on the six-month bills as Russian operators are traditionally more interested in short paper.
At the same time foreign investors were concerned about President Yeltsin's health.
Renat Akchurin, a surgeon likely to perfom a heart operation on Yeltsin, said on Sunday the operation may be delayed or called off altogether.
On Wednesday he said a successful operation should take place after six to eight weeks of delay but bids for Wednesday's auctions had to be made by Tuesday.
The average yield on the three-month bills rose to 69.12 percent from 65.77 percent at the previous auction three weeks ago.
The finance ministry raised a total of 7.3 trillion roubles from the two auctions. It was also repaying 7.0 trillion roubles of maturing six-month bills on Wednesday.
